original.description: Space Weather Centre for Spain Initial Establishment and Core Capability Developments: Part 1This activity will constitute the initial establishment and operation of a Space Weather Centre for affected stakeholders along with underpinning tools, capabilities and procedures required in order to deliver tailored high quality services to end users. Key user groups are expected to include operators of energy transmission systems, satellite operators, the aviation sector, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) and others. The Centre shall operate in close cooperation with ESA's Space weather Service Network with the aim to establish a node that facilitates collaborative actions with network participants while moving progressively towards a structure with a clear operational dimension ableto support the development and delivery of tailored space weather capabilities and services. Particularly the centre will focus on translating complex space weather information from multiple sources into streamlined, actionable information. A colocation of the development and operations teams shall be foreseen with the aim to streamline the R2O process, support team building and to encouragedirect feedback to research, optimising the use of facilities in ESAC.Part 1 shall include: Systematic mapping of end users and establishment of key contact points with users and stakeholders Establishment of a proactive engagement strategy and actions with the identified end users to ensure full understanding of end user needs and operational requirements Development of necessary IT infrastructure, tools and service operation procedures in order to operate the space weather front desk, initially on an 8/5 basis, with on-call support during periods of elevated space weather activity. OoProcedures shall be developed with a view to transitioning into full 24/7 support at the start of a future Part 2 of this activity. Operation of the space weather front desk from KO+3 months for at least 6 months prior to the start of Part 2 handover Development of a space weather dashboard capabilities targeting end users and building on well demonstrated and tested space weather assets, constituting a layer for translating complex technical concepts into an easy-to-use tool for end users. Training for end users including exercises and simulations based on realistic use casesDevelopment of a roadmap for the operational Centre including priority R2O needs and the inclusion of a space weather testbed facility to be used for regional event simulations and training, bringing together stakeholders including end users, operators and domain experts with a focus on optimising the R2O2R pipeline. Support for data and product provision from existing assetsas part of the service provision shall be foreseen where it does not duplicate activities already funded via the Space Safety Programme's pre operational space weather service activities. Operationalisation of certain key models and tools along with their re-deployment within the Centre may be foreseen subject to the necessary licensing agreements with the asset owner. A handover to Part 2of the activity shall be foreseen.

original.description: The increasing deployment of satellites is raising concerns regarding their impact on ground- and space-based astronomical observations and the need to comply with emerging Dark and Quiet Skies (DQS) requirements. Reliable assessment of spacecraft visibility requires accurate knowledge of the optical properties of external spacecraft materials and their environmental degradation over time. However, existing data are limited, fragmented and often unsuitable for consistent spacecraft-level brightness analyses. This activity addresses this gap through the development of a system-integrated European database of optical properties for spacecraft materials with potential observational impacts, including solar arrays, multilayer insulation, thermo-optical coatings, antennas and external optical elements. The activity shall establish the required material datasets, perform dedicated measurement and characterisationcampaigns, and integrate the resulting data into an open-access database supporting DQS compliance assessments and brightness prediction tools. The project targets bringing the technology to TRL 7.

normalized.description: The increasing deployment of satellites is raising concerns regarding their impact on ground- and space-based astronomical observations and the need to comply with emerging Dark and Quiet Skies (DQS) requirements. Reliable assessment of spacecraft visibility requires accurate knowledge of the optical properties of external spacecraft materials and their environmental degradation over time. However, existing data are limited, fragmented and often unsuitable for consistent spacecraft-level brightness analyses. This activity addresses this gap through the development of a system-integrated European database of optical properties for spacecraft materials with potential observational impacts, including solar arrays, multilayer insulation, thermo-optical coatings, antennas and external optical elements. The activity shall establish the required material datasets, perform dedicated measurement and characterisationcampaigns, and integrate the resulting data into an open-access database supporting DQS compliance assessments and brightness prediction tools. The project targets bringing the technology to TRL 7.

original.description: The objective of this activity is to develop a cooling approach for steady state rocket engines to enable the use of more cost-effective materials. This should be achieved with the use of secondary heat exchange.Currently only two cooling approaches are used forrocket motor chamber design. Direct regenerative cooling with the propellants or much simpler radiative cooling. Regenerative cooling recovers energy lost in the radiative approach and offers both higher performance and, wider material options which is possible due to the lower operating temperature.Regenerative cooling is almost never limited by the sensible enthalpy, the temperature rise of the cooling propellants. It is typically limited by local effects in the cooling channel design. These effects come down to two factors the local geometry and the local vapor pressure of the coolant. The geometry is naturally constrained by the need for a rocketchamber shape.In the absence of local geometric options then the local vapor pressure can only be improved for a given propellant by driving up the local static pressure. This rules out many in-space applications where gas pressurized feed systems are the norm, the static pressure is too low. The power for high pressure pumps to regeneratively cool current spacecraft engines would require pumps more than 1.5 kWs. An alternative approach is to design a heat exchanger to transfer the heat from the wall of the combustion chamber to propellant indirectly. This has the advantage of allowing the design of specified cooling rates independent of the geometryor propellant feed conditions. Either end of the exchanger can be designed to operate at specified temperatures. This simplifies the material selection of the chamber and the transfer of energy to the propellant.A fixed temperature exchanger would have none of the limiting factors of a classical regeneratively cooled chamber. It could also simplify start up transient for many larger engine cycles. The more benign operating conditions would also allow for greater reusability; thermal gradients could be more tightly managed and more robust materials could be used, eliminating issues such as plasticity and deformations of the cooling channels. As statedearlier local conditions drive the failure in regenerative engines these are compounded when the engine flow conditions are dynamicwhen throttling. Lander engines tend to require deep throttle rates. Secondary heat exchangers operate outside these constraints and would maintain thermal integrity of deeper throttling designs. Similarly higher performance engine architectures such as aerospikes are inhibited from adoption due to the thermal complexity ofimplementing them compared to classical designs. Various ideas have been considered; however liquid metals are only one potential solution. Active pumping of a secondary coolant would also be feasible.This activity shall focus on the concept of secondary heat exchange design for high performance engine design and demonstrate a secondary heat exchanger unit by firing a representative breadboard. This would allow a greater exploitation of the propellant sensibleenthalpy than current regenerative approaches. In addition, secondary heat exchange would allow low pressure drop designs and enable actively cooled design applications where currently radiative cooling is mandated. Finally secondary heat exchange would allow theenergy to be exploited in other systems if required: repressurization, power recovery, etc. The activity encompasses the following tasks: Analysis of the state of the art of secondary heat exchanger options for combustion chamber applications. Develop and manufacture a breadboard of a secondary heat exchanger for combustion chamber. Demonstrate a secondary heat exchanger for combustion chamber design by firing a representative breadboard with heat exchanger or an appropriatesimulator. Validate the design tools toimplement such a chamber.NOTE: This activity is currently in the GSTP Work Plan but will only be implemented after confirmation offinancial support from Delegations. The final list of participating states will be known at tender issue.
